title: Section 14 Limitation Act — Wrong forum in good faith

content.overview: Time spent diligently and in good faith in a court that could not entertain the matter is excluded from limitation for the later suit.
content.study: Same matter, same defendant, due diligence, good faith, and a defect of jurisdiction or something like it. A hopeless forum-shop does not get 14.

learningObjectives: Apply the provision to a limitation calculation or factual problem.
Distinguish the provision from related limitation rules.
enhancement.definition: Section 14 excludes time spent prosecuting, with due diligence and in good faith, a civil proceeding in a court that cannot entertain it because of jurisdictional defect or a like cause, subject to the statutory conditions.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The provision protects a diligent litigant who pursued the same matter in the wrong forum in good faith; every statutory condition must be satisfied.
enhancement.statutoryFramework: Limitation Act, 1963, Section 14(1) for suits, Section 14(2) for applications and the related sub-sections.
essentialIngredients: Prior and subsequent proceedings must be civil proceedings of the type covered.
The prior proceeding must have been prosecuted with due diligence and in good faith.
The earlier court must have been unable to entertain the matter because of defect of jurisdiction or a like cause.
The proceedings must concern the same matter or the same party and relief as specified by the subsection.
Exclude the qualifying period when computing limitation for the later proceeding.
enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 14 is narrower than a general fairness discretion. The Supreme Court has identified the core conditions: same party/proceeding context, due diligence and good faith, failure because of jurisdiction or a like cause, and sufficient identity between the earlier and later proceedings. Negligence or a materially different claim can defeat the exclusion.
examples: A claimant diligently prosecutes the same civil relief in a court that lacks jurisdiction, discovers the jurisdictional defect, and promptly institutes the proceeding in the competent court. If the statutory conditions are satisfied, the qualifying earlier period may be excluded.
enhancement.distinctions: Section 14 excludes time spent in a qualifying wrong-forum proceeding; Section 5 condones eligible delay; Section 12 deals with specific computational exclusions.

caseLaw.name: M.P. Steel Corporation v. Commissioner of Central Excise
caseLaw.holding: The Supreme Court explained the conditions for Section 14 and recognized that due diligence and good faith are central to excluding time spent in a prior proceeding before a forum unable to entertain it.
caseLaw.relevance: Direct authority on the ingredients of Section 14.

enhancement.problemApplication: Compare the earlier and later proceedings, identify the jurisdictional defect, test due diligence and good faith, and calculate the period to be excluded.
